questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Explore new cultures

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: The country (Germany) and field of study.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: It found it easy to find the information as such, but I found it complicated to get an overall view of the steps required in the process.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: I was welcomed by Studierendenwerk when I picked up the key for my WG. They provided me with very useful information and a number I could call if I was in doubt about something regarding the accommodation.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
questions.answer: The people from all the departments I went to were very nice and helpful. Especially the secretaries and professors at my institute (HCCH) who guided me a lot. I was the first exchange student at the institute and was a lot in dialogue with the them as the process was also new to them. However, in the beginning, I had to wait for their reply (pr. mail) for weeks.

questions.question: How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing through my host institution

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer: As I applied through my host university, the process itself was easy. However, there had been a mistake in their system which meant that I only got my room two weeks before travelling.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: If possible, get a bike so you don't have to stand and wait for public transportation.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: I don't remember it exactly, but I remember it as being only a formula.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: I didn't use any.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: I got accepted in all courses I applied for. The registration process was a bit complicated though as the university's system isn't very intuitive. I got help from a friend that had studied at the university before.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: You can always ask your professor if you want to know more about a course. My experience is that they are only happy to talk about it.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA classes while you were on exchange *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: The level was high and the courses very interesting. I come from another field of study than the one I was taught in at my host university and so many things were new to me. This might also have played a role in my experience of the level of course.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: Because of the smaller courses consisting of less ECTS (e.g. 2, 5 or 8 ECTS), we were fewer people in the class rooms. It created a more intimate atmosphere during the lectures. There was a lot of interaction between professors and students - even in the Vorlesungen - and more physical presence.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: "Immaterielles Erbe: eine Zukunftsressource?" because it was a lecture series featuring several prominent researchers and more. It was very exciting to get an overview of a broad range of knowledge within the field.

questions.answer: Besides the main attractions in Heidelberg, e.g. the castle, the bridge, and the Philosophenweg, visit Kunsthalle in Mannheim, Thingstätte, and all the second-hand bookshops in Heidelberg.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: I found it very easy as I think German and Danish culture have many similarities.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: If you can, join the courses taught in German.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: All the paperwork in public institutions which is digitalized in Denmark.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: I personally really like the German language. And the exchange stay enabled me to speak and improve it. And the beer drinking culture :-)

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
Dont worry, everything will work out in the end, even when things may seem overwhelming at times or if you've missed a deadline. When studying at a German university, the academic calendar is often different from Danish universities. For instance, the spring semester in Germany runs from April to September. This means there are certain deadlines at the University of Copenhagen that you may need to extend. In the end, it all works out as long as you remember to contact your home university. Also, I can only recommend to reach out to a contact person or professor at the host university if you have any doubts or questions, as they are always willing to help. Professors have designated times in their schedules for student consultations (Sprechstunden). Make use of these, as it usually pays off when you need to give a presentation or take an exam, or when you're uncertain about anything. I reached out to one of my professors during my stay because my workload became quite heavy, and they accommodated it.
As mentioned before, participate in Erasmus events as much as you can manage. It's nice to have some companions :-) In Heidelberg, most Erasmus-related communication happens through WhatsApp, so make sure to have it installed and join the group before you leave. This way, you'll be somewhat briefed in advance.
Lastly, I highly recommend taking a language course that the university doesn't offer but promotes once you've been accepted. Not only to improve your language skills, but most of all to meet other international students before the semester starts - these courses typically take place in the month before the semester starts. For the spring semester, for example, it would be in March.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: I find it very important to let coming Erasmus students in Germany, or at least in Heidelberg, know that the German system differs from the Danish, meaning that it is unusual for the German students to take all 30 ECTS per semester. I had to enroll in seven courses in order to acquire 30 ECTS credits, making me the only student in my MA program for that year who had such a heavy course load. As there are many week-to-week papers, presentations, excursions, interviews, and a rule saying that you can only have two days of absence in every course (Fehlertage), I sometimes found it very stressful to keep up. Technically, you have 30 ECTS as you would have back home but due to the existing norm in Germany/Heidelberg, where students have fewer ECTS per semester, they often have more time available for each course. As a result, professors tend to expand the scope of the workload for each course, beyond what the number of ECTS would typically suggest. Therefore, a workload of 30 ECTS can be a lot more extensive than in Denmark, in my experience.
